name: Carlo Mollino
bio: Mollino was Turin's polymath of the illicit: architect, furniture maker, aerobatic pilot, race-car designer, downhill-skiing theorist and, as the world learned after his death, a photographer of thousands of secret Polaroids. His buildings ranged from alpine sled-lift stations to the reborn Teatro Regio, whose hall he shaped like an opening eye; his bent-plywood and glass tables — part skeleton, part woman, he said everything is permissible as long as it is fantastic — now sell for millions. He kept an apartment on the Po that he never lived in, arranging it for years as a warrior's house for the afterlife. Nobody has ever quite decided whether he was a designer with hobbies or an artist whose medium was his own biography; the furniture argues for both.

projects.title: Teatro Regio
projects.blurb: The opera house rebuilt inside its Baroque shell — a purple hall like an eye opening under a cloud of stalactite lights.

projects.title: Casa Mollino
projects.blurb: The secret apartment on the Po he furnished for a decade and never inhabited; now a house-museum by appointment.

projects.title: Stazione Lago Nero

projects.title: Casa del Sole

name: Philip Johnson
bio: Johnson spent seventy years as American architecture's weathervane, kingmaker and gadfly: he named the International Style at MoMA in 1932, built its most transparent monument in his own New Canaan Glass House, then cheerfully betrayed it with the Chippendale top of the AT&T Building and half the granite skylines of the 1980s. His prewar years as a fascist sympathizer were real and are permanently part of the account. As MoMA's first architecture curator and the first Pritzker laureate, he decided for decades who got shows, commissions and dinner invitations at the Century Club. He mattered less as a form-giver than as the discipline's impresario — a role he understood perfectly and never apologized for.

projects.title: Glass House
projects.blurb: His own transparent pavilion on a Connecticut ridge, argued with Mies for the rest of both their lives.

projects.title: 550 Madison (AT&T Building)
projects.blurb: The granite skyscraper with the broken-pediment top — postmodernism's Time-cover moment.

projects.title: Pennzoil Place
projects.blurb: Twin trapezoid towers sliding past each other, ten feet apart.

projects.title: PPG Place
projects.blurb: A neo-Gothic castle complex in mirrored glass for a glass company.

projects.title: Crystal Cathedral
projects.blurb: A televangelist's sanctuary of 10,000 mirrored panes, now a Catholic cathedral.

projects.title: IDS Center
projects.blurb: Minneapolis's zog-cornered tower and its Crystal Court, the city's true living room.

projects.title: Fort Worth Water Gardens

name: Carlo Scarpa
bio: Scarpa never took the Italian professional exam, so the man who taught a century how to join old buildings to new ones practiced, technically, as an unlicensed draftsman from Venice. Trained in glass at Murano and steeped in Wright and Japan, he worked at the scale of the junction — the step, the hinge, the ziggurat molding — and made details carry the meaning other architects assigned to façades. His Castelvecchio in Verona is the permanent textbook of museum design; the Brion Cemetery at San Vito d'Altivole, where concrete is carved like ivory around a garden of water and interlocking circles, is one of the few modern works regularly called sacred. He died in Japan, falling down a flight of concrete stairs, and is buried standing up, wrapped in linen, at the edge of the Brion plot.

projects.title: Brion Cemetery
projects.blurb: A family tomb as a walled garden of water, moss and interlocking circles; his own grave stands at its edge.

projects.title: Castelvecchio Museum
projects.blurb: The renovation that taught the century how new steel and old stone should meet — Cangrande on his floating plinth.

projects.title: Negozio Olivetti

projects.title: Fondazione Querini Stampalia

projects.title: Gypsotheca Canoviana Extension

name: Oscar Niemeyer
bio: It is not the right angle that attracts me, Niemeyer said, but the free and sensual curve — the curve he found in the mountains of his country, in its rivers, and in the body of the beloved woman. Beginning at Pampulha in the 1940s, he bent reinforced concrete into shapes European modernism had never imagined, and with Lúcio Costa drew an entire capital out of the Brazilian savanna. Exiled by the dictatorship, he built for the French Communist Party and the Mediterranean before returning home a national monument himself. He worked until shortly before his death at 104, still drawing curves, still a committed communist, still cheerfully unrepentant about all of it.

projects.title: Brasília Cathedral

projects.title: National Congress
projects.blurb: Dome, saucer and twin towers — the image of the new capital.

projects.title: Niterói Contemporary Art Museum

projects.title: Pampulha Complex

name: Charles & Ray Eames
bio: Charles trained as an architect and Ray as a painter, and together in a Venice, California workshop they dissolved the boundary between architecture, furniture, film and exhibition into a single practice of joyful problem-solving. Their own house — Case Study House No. 8, bolted together from catalogue steel in 1949 — remains the most persuasive argument ever made for industrial parts and personal life coexisting. The molded plywood and fiberglass chairs put serious design in every classroom and airport on earth; the lounge chair put it in every den. Powers of Ten and the IBM exhibitions made them the great explainers of the American century — designers, as Charles said, of the guest-host relationship in everything.

projects.title: Eames House (Case Study No. 8)
projects.blurb: A steel kit-of-parts house in a eucalyptus meadow; the happiest building of the century.

projects.title: Eames Lounge Chair

projects.title: Molded Plywood Chair (LCW)

projects.title: Powers of Ten

name: Gordon Bunshaft
bio: Bunshaft was the designing intelligence inside SOM for four decades, and Lever House — the green glass slab floating on its plaza above Park Avenue in 1952 — was the building that taught corporate America what it wanted to look like. He followed it with a bank you could see straight through, a rare-books library with translucent marble walls, and late in life a doughnut-shaped museum on the National Mall and a desert bank in Jeddah that anticipated a century of Gulf building. Gruff, unquotable and indifferent to theory, he claimed his buildings were simply solved problems; the Pritzker jury disagreed enough to give him the prize in 1988, shared with Niemeyer. His art collection, assembled with the same eye, went to MoMA.

projects.title: Lever House
projects.blurb: The green glass slab-on-plaza that started the curtain-wall era on Park Avenue.

projects.title: Beinecke Library

name: Eero Saarinen
bio: Son of Eliel, raised on the Cranbrook campus his father built, Eero refused a signature style on principle: the style for the job, he said, and gave General Motors a Miesian research Versailles, TWA a concrete bird in flight, and St. Louis a stainless steel arch taller than any monument in the hemisphere. Critics of the fifties scolded him for inconsistency; the decades since have read the same record as range. With Charles Eames he shared a Cranbrook friendship and the organic furniture that came out of it — the womb chair, the tulip pedestal line that abolished the slum of legs. He died at 51 during brain-tumor surgery with ten major buildings unfinished; Dulles, the Arch and the CBS tower all opened without him.

projects.title: TWA Flight Center
projects.blurb: Flight rendered in four concrete shells at Idlewild; now a hotel inside JFK.

projects.title: Gateway Arch
projects.blurb: A 192-meter weighted catenary in stainless steel — the memorial as pure curve.

projects.title: Dulles International Airport
projects.blurb: A hammock of concrete slung between leaning columns; the jet-age terminal solved.

projects.title: General Motors Technical Center
projects.blurb: An industrial Versailles of glazed brick and curtain wall around a 22-acre lake.

projects.title: MIT Chapel

projects.title: Kresge Auditorium

projects.title: Miller House

projects.title: Bell Labs Holmdel

name: Félix Candela
bio: Candela fought for the Spanish Republic, was interned in a French camp, and arrived in Mexico in 1939 with nothing but a Madrid architecture degree and an obsession with the hyperbolic paraboloid — the double-curved surface that can be poured over straight wooden boards. Through his firm Cubiertas Ala he built nearly a thousand shells in two decades: markets, churches, factories and pavilions of concrete sometimes only four centimeters thick. The restaurant at Xochimilco, an eight-petaled groined vault hovering over the canals, is thin-shell construction's most photographed proof. He calculated by hand, distrusted computers, priced his shells cheaper than flat roofs, and late in life lent his geometry to the Oceanogràfic in Valencia, built after his death.

projects.title: Los Manantiales Restaurant
projects.blurb: An eight-petaled concrete flower, four centimeters thin, floating over the canals.

projects.title: Cosmic Rays Pavilion

name: John Lautner
bio: A Taliesin apprentice who came to Los Angeles in 1938 to supervise Wright jobs and never left, Lautner spent fifty years building houses that treat the hillside, the view and the sky as structural materials. His coffee shop Googies gave its name to a whole exuberant roadside style he came to disown; his Chemosphere put an octagonal living room on a single concrete mast over a slope everyone else called unbuildable. The late concrete houses — Elrod in Palm Springs, Sheats-Goldstein in Beverly Crest, Arango over Acapulco Bay — dissolve the boundary between room and horizon so completely that Hollywood has used them as shorthand for power ever since. He considered himself Wright's truest heir and Los Angeles's least understood architect, and was probably right on both counts.

name: Minoru Yamasaki
bio: Born in Seattle to Japanese immigrant parents and worked through college in Alaskan salmon canneries, Yamasaki built a practice on the conviction that modern architecture should offer serenity, surprise and delight rather than shock. His pointed arches, delicate screens and white verticality — New Formalism at its most refined — made him Time-cover famous in 1963. History dealt his reputation the century's strangest hand: he designed both Pruitt-Igoe, the St. Louis housing project whose 1972 demolition was declared the death of modern architecture, and the World Trade Center towers, destroyed in 2001 in the attack that opened another era. Between those two ruins stands a large, graceful, underrated body of work that critics have only recently begun to see again.

projects.title: Pruitt–Igoe
projects.blurb: The 33-building housing project whose televised demolition became modernism's obituary — unfairly, the record now suggests.
